Fishpools
FISH-poolz
n. pl. (stocked pools of still water; the figure for the bride's eyes in the Song)
A compound of fish and pool, Old English pol. In the Song it renders Hebrew berekah, a reservoir or pool — the same word used of the pool of Gibeon and the pool of Siloam.

Biblical Definition

Thine eyes like the fishpools in Heshbon, by the gate of Bathrabbim. The comparison seems odd until one has stood by a reservoir at evening. Heshbon was a Moabite city in the high tableland, and its pools were the still water of a dry country — deep, clear, quiet, gathered where everything around was thirsty, and holding the sky. To say a woman's eyes are like them is to say they are deep and calm and full of light, and that a man could look into them a long while. The Song is a poem of married love, and the church has read it for two thousand years both as that and as a figure of Christ and his people, which is no accident in a Bible that calls the church a bride and the Lord a bridegroom. Pools elsewhere in Scripture are civic infrastructure and the mark of a prudent city — Hezekiah gathered the waters of the lower pool when Assyria came, and Solomon made him pools of water to water the wood. Here the engineering vocabulary is bent to a lover's use. Scripture is not embarrassed by beauty, and has no rule against a husband saying so at length.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): a pool where fish are kept or bred; a small collection of standing water.

expand to see more

FISHPOOL, n. A pool in which fishes are kept.

POOL, n. A small collection of water in a hollow place, supplied by a spring or rain.

RESERVOIR, n. A place where anything is kept in store, particularly a place where water is collected and kept.

COUNTENANCE, n. The whole form of the face, or system of features; the face; look; aspect.

COMELY, a. Handsome; graceful; having a pleasing appearance.

Key Scripture

Song of Solomon 7:4 — "Thy neck is as a tower of ivory; thine eyes like the fishpools in Heshbon, by the gate of Bathrabbim: thy nose is as the tower of Lebanon which looketh toward Damascus."

Ecclesiastes 2:6 — "I made me pools of water, to water therewith the wood that bringeth forth trees:"

Isaiah 22:9 — "Ye have seen also the breaches of the city of David, that they are many: and ye gathered together the waters of the lower pool."

Psalm 42:7 — "Deep calleth unto deep at the noise of thy waterspouts: all thy waves and thy billows are gone over me."

Modern Corruption

Married desire is treated either as the whole of love or as something the devout should be quiet about; the Song is a book of Scripture in which a husband and wife praise each other's bodies at length and God did not edit it out.

expand to see more

A certain strain of piety has always been uneasy with the Song, and has managed the discomfort by allegorizing every line until no bride is left in it. The church fathers found Christ in the fishpools and the tower of ivory, and much of what they saw is genuinely there — Scripture does make marriage a figure of Christ and the church, and Paul says so explicitly of Genesis 2. But the figure only works because the thing figured is real and good. God gave a book to his people in which a husband looks at his wife and describes her at length, and the existence of that book is itself a doctrine.

The age's error is the opposite and louder: desire detached from covenant, made its own justification, and then found to be thin. The Song will not be used that way either. Three times it charges the daughters of Jerusalem not to stir up nor awake love until it please, and it ends by calling love strong as death, jealousy cruel as the grave, a flame with a most vehement flame — and immediately adds that if a man would give all the substance of his house for love, it would utterly be contemned. It cannot be bought and it will not be hurried. Those are covenant words, spoken over fishpools and towers of ivory.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew berekah (H1295), a pool or reservoir; Cheshbon (H2809), Heshbon; ayin (H5869), an eye or a spring; ahavah (H160), love.

expand to see more

Hebrew berekah (H1295) — a pool; the word for Gibeon's pool and Bethesda's counterpart.

Hebrew Cheshbon (H2809) — Heshbon, a city of the Moabite tableland taken by Israel under Moses.

Hebrew ayin (H5869) — an eye, and also a spring of water; the same word does both, which the image exploits.

Hebrew ahavah (H160) — love; love is strong as death.

Hebrew shalhebethyah (H7957) — a most vehement flame, a flame of the LORD; the Song's last word on the subject.

Usage

"“thine eyes like the fishpools in Heshbon” — still water in a dry country."

"“the waters of the lower pool” — the same vocabulary used for a city's defence."

"“I made me pools of water” — the engineering sense, in Solomon's own words."
